content_of_post_to_comment: I used to know a guy who blamed Kafka for his lack of success as a writer. He said that Kafka had written every story there was to write, that every time he tried to write something, somewhere along the way from idea to finished draft to publication, he would realize the story had already been written by Kafka. But the stories he wrote didn’t resemble any of Kafka’s stories at all, on any level (I read many drafts for him). I would say to him, “This is a technological utopia set in the near future. Kafka never wrote anything like that.” He said that I clearly wasn’t paying attention when I read The Castle. That was when we had just met, in Boulder, when we were still in the workshop. I found him annoying at the time, and avoided interacting with him as much as I could. The workshop was called “Ecological Fiction.” Every single session that semester involved at least half an hour of discussion of Kafka. His ability to tie seemingly any topic, no matter how inconsequential or seemingly unrelated, to one of Kafka’s stories, was astounding. I’m sure the professor was exasperated, but what was she supposed to do? Anyway we somehow became friends. I didn’t realize we were friends until later, however, in retrospect. I thought I disliked him for a long time. When the workshop ended I was glad to never have to hear him speak again, but I ran into him in New York, in a coffee shop, I was working on an essay and he appeared next to my table and asked how have I been, could he join me, etc.; I had no choice but to allow him to sit, but I noticed that despite my efforts to dislike him I was happy to see him;
comment: The fascinating part is that Kafka becomes less an influence than a lens: the friend wasn’t finding Kafka in his stories, he was finding Kafka in the act of interpreting everything. A warning and a creative gift at once.
